paragraphs: This paper develops a neural network account of how perceived lightness depends on the spatial organization of a scene. It builds on the FACADE theory's boundary and feature contour systems, connecting the representation of visual regions with the way their lightness is determined.

Two kinds of evidence constrain the model: early encoding of intensity ratios by retinal ganglion neurons, and perceptual findings about lightness remaining stable across different backgrounds. These constraints motivate a contrast negation hypothesis. Its central proposal is that comparisons between regions on the same plane receive greater weight when the visual system determines their lightness.

The model therefore makes three-dimensional relationships relevant to interpreting local contrast. A ratio between two regions matters partly because of how those regions are arranged in the scene. Simulations address the coplanar ratio hypothesis, the Benary cross, and White's illusion. Together, these applications explore whether a shared neural account can connect background constancy with several established lightness phenomena.
neurips-1995-a-neural-network-model-of-3.tldr: A neural model explains lightness judgments by giving greater weight to contrast comparisons between regions on the same plane.

paragraphs: The paper studies overfitting in a deliberately simple setting: one perceptron learns outputs generated by another perceptron with the same architecture. The task is realizable, meaning that the learner's model class contains a solution capable of representing the generating rule. This makes it possible to study overfitting even when the architecture is adequate.

Both perceptrons use sigmoid output functions. Their gain controls the strength of the nonlinearity, providing a way to vary the learning problem while keeping the architectural match intact. The authors observe that strong nonlinearity produces overfitting. Having a correct solution available within the model class therefore does not ensure that learning from examples will generalize well.

The authors explain this behavior and develop a method to avoid it. They give two interpretations of the method: learning with noise and early stopping selected through cross-validation. The simple model provides a tractable setting for understanding behavior that also appears qualitatively in multilayer perceptrons, linking the shape of the learning problem to the need to control training.
neurips-1995-a-realizable-learning-task-.tldr: A perceptron can overfit data generated by an identical architecture when the output nonlinearity is strong.

paragraphs: This paper presents a silicon retina that combines adaptation to background brightness with sensitivity to spatial contrast. Biological retinas motivate the design: they can extract contrast across background intensities spanning five or more orders of magnitude. They adjust their baseline operating level while retaining strong responses to changing input.

The chip also models antagonistic center-surround behavior, in which a region and its surroundings contribute opposing responses. This organization emphasizes differences across an image and helps extract edges. The design draws on receptor adaptation and on center-surround properties associated with both invertebrate retinal cells and the outer plexiform layer of vertebrate retinas.

The authors illustrate how the silicon retina responds across space and time using moving bars. The device contains 59 by 64 pixels on a 6.9 by 6.8 millimeter die, fabricated with a 2-micrometer n-well process. The contribution brings two complementary retinal functions into physical hardware: adjustment to overall illumination and extraction of local image structure as visual input changes.
neurips-1995-adaptive-retina-with-center.tldr: A silicon retina combines brightness adaptation and center-surround responses to extract changing contrast and edges.

paragraphs: This paper applies Freund and Schapire's boosting algorithm to decision trees built using the information ratio criterion from C4.5. The central idea is to construct a sequence of trees in which earlier mistakes influence the training examples presented to later trees. Each tree is trained and pruned using examples filtered through the preceding ensemble.

Examples that previous trees classify incorrectly receive a higher chance of being resampled. This changes the training distribution for the next tree, directing more attention toward cases the ensemble has found difficult. The trees are therefore connected through their training process: the errors of existing members guide the construction of subsequent members.

The authors report results on optical character recognition and on knowledge discovery and data mining problems. The boosted ensemble performs substantially better than single trees, independently trained trees, and trees trained on subsets of the available features. These comparisons support the usefulness of sequentially adapting the training distribution, beyond simply collecting multiple trees into an ensemble.
neurips-1995-boosting-decision-trees-5ad.tldr: Boosting improves decision trees by training successive trees more often on examples that earlier trees misclassified.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a clustering method based on the ferromagnetic Potts model, a physical system whose interacting spins can form aligned groups. The authors use its equilibrium behavior as a computational analogy for dividing data into clusters. Their approach does not assume a particular structure for the probability distribution underlying the data.

The relevant physical model has ferromagnetic, super-paramagnetic, and paramagnetic regions. The method focuses on the super-paramagnetic region, where separate domains of aligned spins appear. These domains provide the organizing idea for clusters: groups emerge through collective behavior within the model. Magnetic susceptibility indicates the temperature range over which these structures remain stable.

An efficient Monte Carlo algorithm estimates both susceptibility and correlations between spins. The correlations measured in the super-paramagnetic region determine how data points are partitioned. Susceptibility thus helps identify the useful operating region, while correlation supplies the grouping information. The contribution is a clustering procedure that turns measurable properties of a simulated physical system into evidence about which data points belong together.
neurips-1995-clustering-data-through-an-.tldr: The method identifies data clusters through stable aligned domains and spin correlations in a simulated Potts model.

paragraphs: This paper examines the practical use of neural network hardware in an autonomous mobile robot. The authors develop a system around EPSILON III, a custom VLSI chip intended specifically for embedded neural applications. The robot serves as a demonstration of how that hardware can support the acquisition of useful behavior.

The demonstration uses an approach the authors call instinct-rule training. With this methodology, the robot acquires basic mobility competence in very few training epochs, or passes through training. The reported outcome connects the learning procedure to an observable robotic capability: the hardware neural system supports the robot in learning how to move.

The authors present this application as evidence of the system's flexibility. Its significance lies in bringing the specialized chip, a training methodology, and an autonomous platform together in a working example. The stated achievement concerns basic mobility and rapid acquisition within that demonstration. It provides a practical account of embedded neural learning, with the robot's acquired competence serving as the central result.
neurips-1995-competence-acquisition-in-a.tldr: A mobile robot using the EPSILON III neural chip learns basic mobility in very few training epochs.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates wake-sleep as a way to fit multilayer stochastic generative models to high-dimensional data. Such a model describes observed data through hidden variables and probabilistic relationships. The question is whether an efficient training method also produces a useful estimate of the data distribution.

Wake-sleep combines top-down generative connections with bottom-up connections that approximate the distribution of hidden units given an observation. The bottom-up pathway provides an approximate account of which hidden configurations could explain the input. It is trained using a simple delta rule, making this recognition pathway part of the algorithm's computational strategy.

The authors compare wake-sleep with Monte Carlo and mean field methods for fitting the same generative model, using both synthetic and real datasets. They also compare against models that are less expressive but easier to fit. These two comparisons address different questions: how well the training algorithm uses a fixed model, and whether a more powerful model is worthwhile in practice. The supplied abstract describes this evaluation without announcing a winning method.
neurips-1995-does-the-wake-sleep-algorit.tldr: The paper compares wake-sleep density estimation with alternative training methods and simpler, easier-to-fit models.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonlinear probability model built around latent variables: quantities that are not directly observed but help explain the data. The motivation is that a relatively small set of underlying factors can combine to produce observations that appear much more complicated. Learning such a representation can expose structure behind that complexity.

The obstacle addressed is the computational effort generally required to train nonlinear latent-variable models. The authors introduce a new algorithm that preserves the general nonlinear capabilities of earlier models while organizing training around expectation-maximization, or EM. The proposed change therefore concerns how a flexible hidden-variable model can be fitted to observations.

The authors demonstrate the model on a toy problem and on measurements used for flow diagnostics in a multiphase oil pipeline. These applications connect the modeling idea to both a simple example and an applied data problem. The contribution is an EM-based training approach for nonlinear density modeling, with demonstrations showing its use in uncovering a compact hidden description of observed data.
neurips-1995-em-optimization-of-latent-v.tldr: A new latent-variable density model retains nonlinear flexibility while using EM-based training.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to optimize a signal's entropy when only a finite collection of observations is available. Those observations cannot uniquely determine the signal's probability density or its entropy. Estimation therefore requires assumptions, such as a chosen functional form or a degree of smoothness, that favor some possible densities over others.

The authors introduce EMMA, a differential learning rule that uses kernel density estimation instead of committing to a parametric density form. Entropy and its derivative are calculated by sampling from the estimated density. The derivative then supplies information for updating the parameters being learned, producing a rule the authors describe as simple and efficient.

The application is detecting and correcting corruption in magnetic resonance images. The authors position this task beyond the reach of existing parametric entropy models. The approach matters because it connects a more flexible density estimate directly to an optimization procedure. It still relies on assumptions needed for density estimation, but those assumptions need not take the form of a fixed parametric distribution.
neurips-1995-empirical-entropy-manipulat.tldr: EMMA uses kernel density estimates to optimize entropy, with an application to detecting and correcting MRI corruption.

paragraphs: The paper introduces family discovery: learning the dimensionality and structure of a parameterized collection of stochastic models. The target is the organization of related models, including how many underlying parameters are needed to describe their variation. This makes the relationships between possible models part of what must be learned.

The task is especially suited to data divided into episodes. Within an episode, samples come from one fixed parameter value; across episodes, the learner can encounter different members of the family. This grouping gives the data a useful organization: observations within an episode characterize one member, while differences between episodes reveal variation within the broader family.

The authors present three algorithms based on surface learning and evaluate them on a parameterized classification task. All are reported to improve performance significantly over two alternatives. The result supports learning the structure shared across related stochastic models when the examples have this episodic organization. The contribution combines a definition of the learning problem with several methods for exploiting it.
neurips-1995-family-discovery-c83fd27600.tldr: Family discovery learns the structure of related stochastic models from episodes generated at individual parameter settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies training in an offline handwriting recognizer that combines a recurrent neural network with a hidden Markov model. A handwritten word is represented as a sequence of frames, each describing a section of the word. For every frame, the network estimates a probability distribution over letters.

The recurrent network is trained with backpropagation through time, a supervised procedure that requires target outputs for each frame. Defining those targets is therefore a central part of building the recognizer: the network needs frame-level guidance even though the input represents a word unfolding across a sequence. The authors present three ways to derive this guidance.

Their new method uses the forward-backward algorithm to obtain the training targets. Among the three methods examined, it produces the recognizer with the lowest error rate. The finding shows that how supervision is constructed can materially affect the performance of the combined system. The contribution centers on using sequence-model computation to improve the targets supplied to the recurrent letter estimator.
neurips-1995-forward-backward-retraining.tldr: Forward-backward-derived training targets give the lowest handwriting recognition error among three target-generation methods.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Gaussian processes as a Bayesian approach to regression. Its motivation comes from a difficulty with neural networks: even a simple prior distribution over network weights can induce a complicated distribution over the functions the network represents. That complication makes Bayesian prediction difficult to carry out.

Gaussian processes place the prior directly over functions. For fixed hyperparameters, the predictive Bayesian calculation can then be performed exactly through matrix operations. This gives the approach a clear computational advantage in how prediction is expressed: the function-level prior leads to a tractable calculation once its controlling settings are specified.

The authors test two ways of handling those hyperparameters. One uses optimization to choose their values; the other averages over them using Hybrid Monte Carlo. This distinction matters because exact prediction at a fixed setting and accounting for uncertainty over settings are separate tasks. Both approaches are tested on several challenging problems, with results described as excellent. The paper thus presents direct function priors as a practical route to Bayesian regression.
neurips-1995-gaussian-processes-for-regr.tldr: Gaussian process priors enable exact Bayesian regression calculations at fixed hyperparameters using matrix operations.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way for Boolean circuits to perform real-valued computation while naturally extending their existing Boolean behavior. The construction connects discrete circuit elements with continuous neural computation. In particular, threshold gates receiving multiple inputs are shown to behave like a hardware implementation of continuous neural networks.

The authors analyze the resulting systems using Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension and sample-size bounds. This connects the expressive capacity of the model class to the amount of training data required for generalization. The analysis therefore addresses a statistical question alongside the circuit construction: what learning requirements follow from this particular way of implementing real-valued functions?

The paper reports sample-size results described as the best known for a real-valued neural network in its setting. Experiments support the conclusion that these networks require substantially fewer samples than sigmoidal networks. The contribution joins an implementation-oriented model with theoretical and experimental evidence about learning from data, showing how the choice of computational units can affect the amount of training evidence needed.
neurips-1995-generalisation-of-a-class-o.tldr: A real-valued extension of Boolean circuits yields neural networks with favorable sample-size bounds and supporting experimental results.

paragraphs: A scalp EEG measurement contains activity spread from a broad brain area because electrical signals pass through tissues with different resistivities. The paper argues that this spatial mixing introduces no significant time delays, making independent component analysis a suitable approach to separating the recorded signals. It treats identifying distinct sources separately from locating them in the brain.

The authors apply ICA to EEG and event-related potentials recorded during a sustained auditory detection task. Their initial results show training is insensitive to different random seeds. They also report separation of recognizable artifacts, including electrical line noise, muscle activity, and eye movements, from other signal components.

ICA further isolates overlapping phenomena such as alpha and theta bursts and spatially separable event-related potential components into different output channels. Changes in residual correlation between those channels can track changes in EEG and behavioral state. The findings support ICA as a way to disentangle mixed recordings and follow their changing organization, while preserving the distinction between separating activity and establishing its anatomical origin.
neurips-1995-independent-component-analy.tldr: ICA separates EEG artifacts and overlapping neural activity, while residual channel correlations help track changes in signal and behavioral state.

paragraphs: This paper describes an alphanumeric handwriting recognition module built around two neural networks. The first finds individual characters within a field containing letters and numbers; the second classifies those characters. Both operate on Gabor projections derived from the original pixel images, a representation reported to improve recognition and resistance to noise.

The system also includes substantial application-specific postprocessing, extending its purely numeric counterpart. It runs on specialized parallel hardware at 80 characters per second per board and was installed at the United Kingdom's Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency. The contribution therefore covers a complete deployed recognition system, including character finding, classification, postprocessing, and hardware execution.

Without rejecting inputs, the reported success rate exceeds 96% per character and reaches 85% per field. Rejecting approximately 20% of fields raises success on the accepted material to 99.8% per character and 99.5% per field. These figures show why both evaluation levels matter: an entire field can fail when an individual character is wrong. They also make the tradeoff between coverage and recognition accuracy explicit.
neurips-1995-kodak-lmagelinktm-ocr-alpha.tldr: Kodak's deployed handwriting system combines two neural networks, Gabor features, and postprocessing, reaching 99.5% field accuracy when roughly 20% of fields are rejected.

paragraphs: Fine manipulation tasks such as grasping and assembly require a robot to account for its contact with objects. This paper develops a method that learns movement from measurements while explicitly estimating the current contact state. The approach requires little or no prior knowledge, making contact estimation part of the learned model.

The contact state is represented as the hidden state of a discrete hidden Markov model. Each state has its own movement parameters, while transitions between states depend on control and are modeled using parameterized functions of the measurements. The authors show that transition parameters and movement parameters can be estimated together from the observed data.

Training uses a variant of expectation-maximization. The expectation step is computed exactly, but an exact maximization step is generally unavailable, so gradient ascent is used to increase likelihood. This is a stated computational compromise within the learning procedure. The resulting framework connects changing contact conditions with movement dynamics, allowing a model of fine motion to include an estimate of the otherwise hidden contact state.
neurips-1995-learning-fine-motion-by-mar.tldr: A hidden Markov model learns fine movement and contact states jointly through an EM variant with gradient-based parameter updates.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational account of rodent navigation that brings together representations of location, heading, and movement-based position updating. Its place-cell analogue represents where the animal is, while its head-direction analogue represents which way it faces independently of location. Navigation requires these representations to remain consistently aligned.

The authors examine this coordination through simulations of interactions between the place and head-direction systems. The simulations address observations of hippocampal place-cell responses when visual cue cards in a cylindrical arena are duplicated or rotated. Such manipulations change the environmental information available for aligning the animal's internal spatial representations.

The supplied experimental description concerns rats repeatedly entering a familiar arena at the same location without prior disorientation. Within this setting, the authors report that interactions between the modeled systems can account for observed responses to cue changes. The significance is an explanation based on coordination between internal representations: place-cell behavior is interpreted in relation to the heading system and the broader navigational model.
neurips-1995-modeling-interactions-of-th.tldr: Simulated interactions between place and head-direction systems account for rat place-cell responses to altered visual cues.

paragraphs: The paper describes analytical methods for understanding how recurrent neural networks evolve over time near saturation. It covers both symmetric and nonsymmetric networks, so its scope includes different relationships between reciprocal connections. The object of analysis is the network's dynamics, including the activity that occurs as its state changes.

The central methodological feature is explicit treatment of correlations between postsynaptic potentials. These are the input potentials received by neurons through their connections. Accounting for correlations means that relationships among these inputs enter the analysis, rather than being discarded when describing the network's behavior. This is the detail the authors identify as enabling reliable predictions.

The stated payoff is prediction of transients: the time-dependent behavior that occurs during the network's evolution. Such predictions describe the course of activity, beyond specifying an eventual state. The contribution is therefore an analytical account in which correlated neuronal inputs help determine temporal behavior. Its stated setting is networks near saturation, and the claimed reliability concerns transient predictions within that setting.
neurips-1995-modern-analytic-techniques-.tldr: Explicitly accounting for correlated postsynaptic potentials enables reliable transient predictions for recurrent networks near saturation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes predictive Q-routing, a memory-based reinforcement learning method for adapting network traffic routes. It targets two weaknesses of Q-routing: difficulty refining routing policies when network load is low, and difficulty learning new optimal policies as load decreases. Both concern adjustment when traffic conditions become less demanding.

The method retains the best experiences it has learned and reuses them according to a prediction of the traffic trend. Memory therefore serves a selective, forward-looking role. The approach connects previously successful experience with an estimate of how conditions are changing, so that past learning can inform routing decisions under a different load.

The authors evaluate predictive Q-routing in simulations spanning multiple network topologies and traffic conditions. They report improvements over Q-routing in both learning speed and adaptability. These findings support the proposed combination of selective memory and traffic-trend prediction. The contribution addresses how a routing learner can respond to changing conditions, especially the low-load and decreasing-load cases identified as problems for the earlier method.
neurips-1995-predictive-q-routing-a-memo.tldr: Predictive Q-routing reuses its best experiences according to traffic trends, improving simulated learning speed and adaptability over Q-routing.

paragraphs: The paper models head-direction cells, neurons whose activity indicates the direction a rat faces within its surroundings. Their directional preference is independent of the animal's location. The quantity being represented is heading relative to the environment, rather than simply the position of the head relative to the body.

The authors propose a biophysical model in which a circuit involving the thalamus and cortex computes heading by integrating the head's angular velocity over time. In plain terms, the circuit accumulates turning information to update direction. This provides a proposed mechanism connecting a changing movement signal with an ongoing representation of orientation.

The model is implemented in the NEURON simulator and produces testable predictions about the structure and function of the head-direction circuit. The contribution is thus a simulated biological mechanism for a navigational computation, together with predictions that could be examined experimentally. The results suggest how such a circuit might work; the claim presented is a mechanistic proposal supported through modeling.
neurips-1995-simulation-of-a-thalamocort.tldr: A biophysical simulation proposes that a thalamocortical circuit computes heading by accumulating head-turning velocity over time.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the long-run behavior of a convergent unlearning algorithm for a Hopfield-type neural network. Its focus is probabilistic: the authors consider the chances of different asymptotic outcomes, meaning the behaviors approached as the algorithm continues. The analysis therefore concerns which eventual outcomes occur and how likely they are.

The stated setting uses unbiased random patterns. That assumption defines the pattern population for the analysis and gives the probability questions a specific scope. The paper's subject is the behavior of the unlearning procedure under those conditions, with attention to the possible outcomes rather than only the fact that the algorithm converges.

The central reported result is that failed unlearning leads to total memory breakdown. This makes the failure outcome consequential for the network's memory as a whole. It also shows why convergence and successful memory behavior must be distinguished: an algorithm's eventual outcome still needs to be assessed for what it preserves. The paper contributes a probability-based examination of those outcomes and a strong characterization of failure.
neurips-1995-some-results-on-convergent-.tldr: For unbiased random patterns, the paper analyzes unlearning outcomes and shows that failed unlearning causes total memory breakdown.

paragraphs: The paper studies large stochastic control problems using compact approximations to the cost-to-go function, which represents expected future cost. A variant of value iteration updates these approximations. Although compact representations make large problems more manageable, the authors note that such approximate dynamic programming methods can be unstable in general.

They identify a class of problems where convergence and controlled error bounds are guaranteed. The representation must be linear in its parameters, and the dynamic programming operator must be a contraction in Euclidean norm when applied to functions in the chosen class. Informally, the contraction requirement means that the update shrinks differences measured in that norm.

The authors provide a special case satisfying the condition through locality of transitions in the state space. This ties the guarantee to the structure of the control problem as well as the approximation scheme. The result gives a concrete route to stable approximate value iteration, with the convergence and error claims depending on the stated contraction assumption.
neurips-1995-stable-linear-approximation.tldr: Linear approximate value iteration has convergence and error guarantees under a Euclidean contraction condition satisfied by a local-transition special case.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a representation in which a signal's components are statistically independent. Such a factorial representation expresses the joint distribution through separate component distributions. The problem becomes more demanding when the statistical relationships between signal components are nonlinear, because a linear transformation may not capture the structure that connects them.

The authors position the task as an extension of principal component analysis and independent component analysis. In their account, PCA handles linear correlations in Gaussian signals, while ICA addresses linear dependencies without requiring Gaussian distributions. Nonlinear component analysis targets the further case in which dependencies themselves require a nonlinear transformation.

The proposed solution is a feed-forward nonlinear map built from explicit symplectic transformations and designed to conserve information. The method also handles non-Gaussian output distributions by considering higher-order statistics of individual coordinates. These two elements address different aspects of the goal: transforming nonlinear relationships and describing output components beyond Gaussian behavior. The contribution is a proposed information-conserving route to extracting statistically independent features from nonlinearly dependent signals.
neurips-1995-symplectic-nonlinear-compon.tldr: The paper proposes information-conserving symplectic transformations to extract independent components from nonlinearly dependent signals.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why networks using Gaussian or bump-like activation functions had shown encouraging experimental behavior. The motivating reports describe networks needing fewer hidden units and layers and often learning faster than sigmoid-based networks. The authors approach this question through a simplified mathematical model of representational capacity.

Their model is a hyper-ridge network: a perceptron-like unit with a ridge activation function and no hidden units. They study how many ways it can divide a collection of points into two classes. These possible binary labelings, called dichotomies, provide a way to compare the expressive abilities of the hyper-ridge and an ordinary perceptron.

The comparison depends on the relationship between the number of points and their dimension. In the infinite-dimensional limit, the two models have identical capacity. For the finite point-to-dimension regime discussed as practically relevant, the authors instead derive a ratio between their dichotomy counts. The result shows why equality in a limiting capacity calculation need not capture the representational differences relevant to the motivating network experiments.
neurips-1995-the-capacity-of-a-bump-d602.tldr: A capacity analysis compares ridge and ordinary perceptrons, showing that their dichotomy counts depend on the point-to-dimension regime.

paragraphs: The paper presents SEE-EAGLE, a modular neural system that lets a person guide robot pick-and-place actions by pointing. It begins with stereo pairs of color video images and recognizes the person's hand gesture. The gesture is then used to identify the target object and determine its location in Cartesian coordinates.

Several networks divide the visual and geometric work among modules. Their tasks include image segmentation, hand localization, estimation of three-dimensional pointing direction, object recognition, and coordinate transformations. Color-sensitive networks help determine the position of the referenced object. The functions of all modules are learned from data examples, linking the stages into one operational system.

The robot uses the resulting position to grasp the object, while a second pointing gesture can specify where to place it. The reported localization accuracy is one centimeter within a 50 by 50 centimeter workspace. In the authors' environment, this is sufficient to pick and place objects at arbitrary positions within that area, demonstrating a complete path from human gesture to robotic action.
neurips-1995-visual-gesture-based-robot-.tldr: SEE-EAGLE combines learned vision modules to turn human pointing gestures into robot pick-and-place actions with one-centimeter localization accuracy.
